newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukrainians, divided over past, welcome Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Ukrainians, divided over past, welcome Yeltsin.

text.p: People in this sleepy, dusty town where Ukraine and Russia concluded a union more than 300 years ago welcomed Russian President Boris Yeltsin's scheduled trip on Friday to sign a friendship treaty.
But they seemed less sure about the wisdom of Ukrainian hetman (Cossack leader) Bohdan Khmelnytsky, hailed in Soviet history books for joining Ukraine to Russia "eternally" in 1654.
In the six-year-old independent Ukraine, he is seen at best as a naive victim who sacrificed Ukraine's independence to conclude a strategic military alliance.
The fates of what were once parts of a united though weak Slavonic kingdom separated after Mongol hordes rampaged through the region which they dominated from the 13th to the 15th centuries.

Moscow, which shook off Mongol rule in 1480, started building a centralised state while the southern parts, which later became known as Ukraine, were the scene of rivalry between Moscovia, Poland and Crimean Turkish rulers for many years.
On January, 18, 1654 Khmelnytsky called a meeting of the Cossacks' elite and the tsar was accepted as overlord.

"On that day, drummers summoned the populace to the town square where the hetman spoke of Ukraine's need for an overlord, presented the four potential candidates -- the Polish king, the Tatar khan, the Ottoman sultan, and the Muscovite tsar," writes Ukraine's History by Professor Orest Subtelny.
"He declared that the Orthodox tsar was the best suited for the role. Pleased that the choice had fallen on an Orthodox ruler, the crown responded favorably to the hetman's speech."
Now goats graze the grass and dozens of ducks wander around the square at Pereyaslav where a monument was erected in 1954 by Soviet rulers to remember the Cossack pledge to Russia.
The hetman, Muscovite ambassador and Cossacks are captured in stone with a bronze sign reading "May we be united forever".
Nearby the site of the planned Museum of Historic Pereyaslavska Rada (council) looks abandoned.
"They have been building it for 18 years -- it looks unlikely they will finish it," Inna Horbatyuk, a woman in her 50s passing the square, said.
Locals in the town, 90 km (50 miles) southeast of the capital Kiev, were unsure if Khmelnytsky did the right thing.
"Ukraine must live separately. Khmelnytsky was wrong. Ukraine lost everything later. Now Russia wants the Black Sea Fleet, but it's ours," said Olexiy Khytry, 18, a local student.
He was referring to the Black Sea Fleet based on Ukraine's Crimean peninsula, which has been split between Moscow and Kiev with the Russians getting the lion's share.

"Bohdan was right. Ukraine had never been independent and was always ruled from outside -- by Poles, by Turks...People never lived well. It was only good under Russia," said Tamara Levchenko, in her 60s.
"Russians didn't seize us, rather we wanted union with them. In case of danger we'll again look to Russia."
Ukrainian-Russian relations when they were joined in an empire and later in the Soviet Union have not always been warm.
Tsarist Russia banned the Ukrainian language in 1863 and the Ukrainian People's republic of 1918-1920 was crushed by Bolsheviks and denounced by Soviet textbooks as "bourgeois".
The mass famine, set by Kremlin dictator Jozef Stalin in 1932-1933, when 7.5 million of Ukrainians died, is now viewed as an attempt by Moscow to annihilate the Ukrainian nation.
"Bohdan Khmelnytsky had no choice but to conclude a treaty with Russia -- who knew things would work out differently," Volodymyr Kravchenko, a farmworker, said.

"But this treaty will give us a lot -- I think Yeltsin will give some aid, money," he added, referring to a friendship treaty Yeltsin and President Leonid Kuchma are due to sign on Saturday during the Russian leader's first state visit.

"I am pleased we will again be friends with Russia. We are so close and lived together for so long. We do not differ much from the Russians -- except the ones in the Far East and Siberia," Borys Pecheny, 72, said.
"But Ukraine should be independent. Russia used to be aggressive, but now looks more or less fine. We trust Yeltsin."
